prize_parts.citation: For discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and its active form, which enabled incretin-based therapies for type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: All six openings ranked GLP-1 first, but unanimity is not the argument. The scientific chain is unusually complete: proglucagon processing and the incretin effect (Holst), the biologically active truncated GLP-1(7-36) peptide (Mojsov), and receptor biology with gut, pancreatic and central actions (Drucker). This led to long-acting agonists with large independent outcome trials in diabetes, obesity, and cardiovascular and renal disease. The mechanism is settled, the clinical scale is very large, and the benefit has been replicated across drug classes for over a decade, so recognition is mature rather than premature. As a neurologist I also note that the central appetite-circuit action ties the discovery to neuroscience, though that is not why I rank it first.
statement.case_against: The attribution is the real weakness. Priority for identifying the active GLP-1 peptide is contested, with Habener and colleagues outside the supplied names, and a three-person cap forces us to leave out Lotte Bjerre Knudsen, whose long-acting analogue development is what actually reached patients. A prize for the physiology can look as if it passes over the drug-development step. Naming Mojsov also depends on a historical judgement I cannot verify from the supplied record.

responses.point: Proposes Drucker, Holst and Mojsov, leaves Knudsen out as more drug-development oriented, and ranks optogenetics second as a field-wide methodological advance.
responses.response: I agree on the trio for B021, but I would not treat Knudsen's exclusion as obvious. The citation should be worded around the physiology and the active peptide so it does not claim to reward drug development, and we should state openly that this is a choice. On optogenetics, I accept the methodological impact but I am not persuaded that a six-person crowded claim can be resolved into a defensible trio, and I would keep it as an alternative rather than a co-prize.

responses.point: Ranks CAR-T second with June and Sadelain only, because the CAR-specific decisive work is theirs, and notes the Rosenberg question and the missing Eshhar credit.
responses.response: I share the concern about Rosenberg: his adoptive cell therapy work is foundational, but it is a different achievement from costimulated CAR design. I differ on whether a June and Sadelain pair is safe. Leaving out Eshhar, who originated the chimeric receptor, is a serious fairness problem that a two-name pair does not fix. That is why I keep CAR-T as an alternative and not as a second part alongside GLP-1.

responses.point: Highlights that the Mojsov priority dispute and the question of rewarding physiology versus drug development (Knudsen) are unresolved, and that Knudsen is the most natural fourth name.
responses.response: This is the sharpest challenge to my preferred configuration and I do not think it is answered. If the committee concludes that the therapeutic step must be recognised, the choice is between Knudsen and Mojsov, and I currently lean towards keeping Mojsov because the active peptide is the basis for everything downstream. I would want the final round to test whether a physiology-centred citation is acceptable to four members before we lock it in. I also note that Perlmann and I have co-authored, which does not affect this judgement.

responses.point: Ranks anti-TNF (Feldmann and Maini) second as a clean two-person, long-overdue bench-to-bedside advance in autoimmune medicine, noting her own field-familiarity bias.
responses.response: I take the point that the attribution of B032 is cleaner than almost anything else on the list, and that is a real virtue. My reservation is conceptual: the cytokine-blockade concept is a translation of previously known TNF biology, so the committee has to decide whether it fits as an independent discovery. I did rank it eighth, not higher, for that reason, but I would support it as a second part if the group prefers two achievements. It would not fit within the three-person limit alongside a three-person GLP-1 part, so that would require trimming GLP-1.

uncertainties: Whether the active GLP-1 peptide credit (Mojsov versus Habener and others) can be defended on the evidence we have
Whether the committee wants to reward drug development (Knudsen) and, if so, who yields within the three-person limit
Whether a methodological tool such as optogenetics fits the remit as strongly as a therapy, and how to select three of six names
Whether to add a second achievement at all, given the three-person cap
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile for the shortlisted candidates. I have co-authored with Thomas Perlmann on dopamine neuron topics, which is a colleague relationship and not a connection to any shortlisted candidate. I worked with Paul Greengard as a postdoctoral fellow, and he is not a candidate.
